transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Time: 14:00 PST
Duration: 1h15m
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sara Lin (Redwood SE), Priya Natarajan (QuasarAI - Head ML Infra), Daniel Park (QuasarAI - Senior ML Eng), Lidia Gomez (QuasarAI - CTO), Owen Reed (QuasarAI - DevOps)

Summary (auto): quick deep-dive into GPU runtime profiling across TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, kernel selection behavior, CUDA graphs, KV cache warmup, batching strategies and quantization tradeoffs; agreed to run pilot benchmarks inside QuasarAI VPC with raw traces.

00:00:00 - Avery: alright thanks everyone for joining, i think we have an hour fifteen, wanted to run a deep dive on the gpu runtime profiling stuff we discussed last week and show some side-by-side traces from tllm and vllm, and then go into cuda graphs, kv cache behavior, batching, and quantization.
00:00:22 - Priya: thanks, yeah excited, we've been hitting some latency tail issues at 99th with our 13B model and also curious about how caching will behave in steady state vs cold starts.
00:00:35 - Marco: great, i'll share my screen in a sec, real quick housekeeping - we'll use some shorthand, TensorRT-LLM as t-llm, and vLLM the open runtime. note that some names might be transcribed weird in the meeting notes.
00:00:50 - Lidia: fine by me.

00:01:10 - Marco: ok first slide, high-level: kernel selection - t-llm uses TensorRT kernels that are often fused for attention + ffn patterns, while vllm (with pytorch kernels) favors pointwise kernels and has more opportunity to benefit from cuda graph capture across the whole sequence generation loop. that means different perf profiles across batch size and sequence lengths.
00:01:40 - Daniel: can you elaborate on "fused" there? like does it change kv cache layout?
00:01:44 - Marco: good question. so tensorRT fused attention tends to reorganize memory to favor contiguous q/k/v blocks and uses custom kernels for rotary and rmsnorm. kv cache layout can be different \u2014 t-llm's kernels prefer packed KV layout optimized per-head, whereas vLLM/KV cache (the python-side) ends up with separate tensors per layer that are appended to. that affects the cost of cache reads during generation.
00:02:10 - Owen: so does that mean warmup is faster in one or the other?
00:02:13 - Marco: in our traces warmup throughput often looks better for vllm when you use cuda graphs to amortize launch overhead, but t-llm shows better steady-state per-token latency for long sequences because of fused kernels and lower memory copies.

00:03:05 - Marco: i'm pulling up a flamegraph -- this is a 13B LLM run with seq len 1024, beam size 1, temperature 0.9, batch size 4. first trace is vLLM captured with cuda graphs enabled for the inner loop. you can see lots of runtime overhead from many small kernels (softmax, matmul pointwise) but cuda graphs collapsed launch overhead; however memory copies around kv cache still show up.
00:03:40 - Priya: we're using mixed precision already, AMP, with 16-bit, but we haven't tried 4-bit quantization in prod. do you think that will change these profiles?
00:03:50 - Marco: yes. quantization changes kernel choices and memory footprint, often reducing memory bandwidth pressure and enabling larger effective batch sizes. with 4-bit you can see a change in how attention kernels execute \u2014 some fused kernels become less optimal because they rely on FP16 math. TensorRT-LLM has dedicated int4/int8 kernels that are highly optimized but require calibration and can change latency characteristics.
00:04:20 - Sara: i'll add that we saw reduced peak memory by ~40% in our internal runs when switching to 4-bit, so batching options open up, but you might need to validate output quality per prompt set.

00:05:10 - Marco: next slide \u2014 cuda graphs. we instrumented both runtimes, and for vLLM the best win came from capturing the whole generation step (token loop) when the shape is stable; it removes enqueue latency for many small kernels. for t-llm the wins are smaller because the kernel count is already lower due to fusion. if your workload has variable sequence length or a lot of non-autoregressive ops, cuda graph capture is trickier.
00:05:40 - Daniel: variable seq len in our production traffic is pretty common, users submit short queries and long context occasionally. how fragile is graph capture?
00:05:47 - Marco: it's sensitive \u2014 cuda graph capture requires deterministic launches with matching shapes/streams; if you have a lot of shape churn, you need multiple captured graphs and a dispatcher. that adds complexity. we often use a hybrid: capture common shapes (like 128, 512, 1024) and fall back to dynamic path otherwise.

00:07:00 - Priya: about kv cache eviction and prefix cache, we've seen spikes when we flush caches on model update. any recommendations?
00:07:09 - Marco: two patterns: prefix caching (cache common prompts or system messages at the top) reduces repeated compute, and persistent KV cache across requests using request routing to same device can eliminate reloading. for updates, we recommended rolling updates with cache warmers \u2014 spin up a canary replica, warm the cache with representative prompts, and then shift traffic.
00:07:35 - Avery: note that Redwood platform supports sticky routing and cache pre-warming tooling as part of Dedicated/Private deployments, we can help automate that warmup.
00:07:45 - Lidia: how about network egress \u2014 if we run in our VPC the traffic between clients and model endpoints is internal, but what's the overhead for cache sync or logs?
00:07:55 - Sara: for Private deployment we co-locate the inference nodes inside the VPC where clients call endpoints; there's minimal network egress. logs/audit can be configured to ship asynchronously to your SIEM with batching to minimize latency impact.

00:08:30 - Marco: back to kernel selection: here's an example where t-llm's attention+ffn fusion reduces total kernel count by ~35% and lowers per-token latency by ~15% at batch size 8 seq 1024. but at small batch sizes (1-2) the difference narrows because launch overhead dominates and vLLM with cuda graphs can catch up.
00:09:05 - Daniel: any numbers around tail latency? our 99.9% is the thing that keeps us up.
00:09:11 - Marco: in our internal tests at QPS 200 with bursty arrivals, t-llm had 99th around 220ms and 99.9th 340ms on A100-80GB running 13B with batch pooling; vLLM w/graphs had 99th 260ms and 99.9th 480ms, but vLLM had faster cold-start median when graph capture matched shape. your mileage will vary with request distribution.
00:09:45 - Priya: ok that matches what we see-ish, our 99th is around 300ms but spikes higher during deploys.

00:10:10 - Marco: for kernel-level debugging, we used Nsight compute and custom NVTX ranges; i'll attach the per-kernel timeline. one interesting artifact is that some attention kernels in t-llm do larger GEMM ops that show up as a single long matmul call \u2014 that's a win for throughput but makes it hard to isolate sub-op regressions.
00:10:40 - Priya: you mentioned memory copies earlier; are those host-to-device or device-device?
00:10:45 - Marco: mostly device-device, and some device-host for logging/checkpointing. many copies are for KV cache reorganizations between layers \u2014 a cost that can be reduced with custom allocator/pool and avoiding per-token reallocation.

00:11:30 - Daniel: on batching: does Redwood favor static batching or dynamic continuous batching?
00:11:36 - Marco: Redwood's runtime uses continuous batching with adaptive timeouts \u2014 it aims to maximize utilization while meeting latency SLOs. we also allow static batching profiles where you reserve a specific batch size for predictable throughput. for Quasar's workload with burstiness we'd likely recommend adaptive continuous batching with a conservative target latency to avoid long tail.
00:12:00 - Owen: what about multi-tenancy? if we run Dedicated but host other teams, how do you isolate noisy neighbors?
00:12:04 - Sara: Dedicated deployments give you GPU pools and scheduling policies; we can do tenant-aware scheduling and cgroup-like GPU isolation. for strict isolation, Private on-prem with dedicated nodes is the option.

00:12:40 - Marco: switching gears \u2014 quantization. there's int8, int4, and FP16. we recommend FP16 as a low-risk first step, then int8 with calibration, and int4 for aggressive cost reduction if quality tests pass. TensorRT-LLM often has more mature int8/int4 kernels out of the box, while vLLM relies on third-party quant libs which can be more experimental.
00:13:15 - Priya: sample-quality checks \u2014 how do you validate? we have a suite of prompts and a small human eval team.
00:13:22 - Avery: that's perfect. we integrate quality monitoring tied to prompt sets and run diff comparisons against baseline; Redwood Optimize can auto-suggest quant configurations that maintain pass thresholds. we'll need your evaluation set.

00:14:10 - Marco: here's a more detailed trace \u2014 i'm zooming into a single token generation: note NVTX label spikes at decoder layer 10 where we see a memcpy+transpose for kv gather in vLLM; that accounts for ~12% of time. in t-llm that step is fused into the attention kernel so you don't see the memcpy but the matmul slightly larger.
00:14:45 - Daniel: if we change kv layout to packed interleaved, can we avoid that memcpy?
00:14:50 - Marco: yes but it requires changing how you append and read KV \u2014 some model code expects the per-layer per-step append pattern. TensorRT-LLM kernels assume packed layout, so moving to that layout can reduce copies but requires a conversion at load time or adapter.

00:15:30 - Lidia: ops question \u2014 do you recommend we run benchmarks in our VPC or can you run them on Redwood Hosted and still be accurate?
00:15:37 - Marco: for kernel-level profiling and memory layouts, hosted runs are fine, but network and VPC-specific differences (eg. private EFA or custom NICs) make in-VPC runs more representative. plus if you want to validate Private deployment networking and security, we should run inside your VPC.

00:16:10 - Marco: i'm going to show a parity comparison table: columns: median latency, 95th, 99th, 99.9th, tokens/sec, memory usage. rows: t-llm fp16, t-llm int8, vllm fp16 (graphs), vllm fp16 (no graphs). notice int8 reduces memory ~30-40% and improves tokens/sec, but sometimes increases p99 due to calibration/runtime conversions.
00:16:45 - Priya: curious about autop small-batch optimization in t-llm \u2014 can it switch kernels dynamically?
00:16:50 - Marco: yes to an extent. we have hybrid kernel selector that picks small-batch kernels for some layers and fused kernels for others based on heuristics like batch*seq and head dim. but switching mid-run can cause jitter so it's typically done per model/config.

00:17:30 - Sara: question from our SRE perspective: what telemetry do we need to capture to reconstruct these issues?
00:17:35 - Marco: NVTX ranges, per-kernel durations, CUDA graph capture IDs, memory allocator stats, KV cache hit/miss counters, and request routing metadata (which replica handled request, cache state) \u2014 those allow you to tie a single request to kernel timelines.
00:17:55 - Owen: is the NVTX/trace volume significant? any suggestions to keep observability low cost?
00:17:59 - Marco: sample traces at 1/1000 requests and aggregate counters at 1s granularity. high-fidelity per-kernel traces on demand for failed/slow requests. store raw traces in compressed form; we can help set retention policies.

00:18:40 - Marco: switching to an example of dynamic batching: we simulated a bursty 2-minute window with median seq 64 but tail at 1024. continuous batching increased overall throughput but increased p99 for short requests; so we tuned the batching timeout and the max batch size, and introduced a fast-path for single-token low-latency requests.
00:19:10 - Daniel: can that fast-path bypass kv cache?
00:19:13 - Marco: no, you still use kv cache, but you route to an instance with a smaller batching delay and smaller prefetch. basically, shape-aware routing.

00:19:45 - Priya: any notable differences in power/thermal behavior on infra when comparing these runtimes?
00:19:50 - Marco: fused kernels in t-llm tend to be more power efficient because they reduce memory traffic; vLLM's many small kernels incur more SM stalls and can increase energy per token slightly. depends on hardware generation.

00:20:20 - Lidia: on security/compliance \u2014 if we run Private, how do you handle KMS integration for model keys and telemetry?
00:20:28 - Avery: Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations; keys never leave your control plane, and telemetry can be routed to your audit log endpoints. we'll share a security checklist.

00:21:05 - Marco: next, i'll show an artifact from a CUDA graph run where we logged the capture node sequence. one gotcha: if your model uses dynamic control flow inside the loop (eg. early-exit or variable work per layer) graphs will fail to capture. in those cases we fallback to JIT-compiled dynamic kernels or use partial graph capture.
00:21:35 - Daniel: our model has some conditional logic for certain tokens (safety checks) - that may break capture.
00:21:41 - Marco: yep, that's a common pattern \u2014 we either isolate the conditional work outside the hot loop or build multiple graphs for the common variants.

00:22:10 - Marco: i'm going to pull up some raw nvprof/trace screenshots \u2014 you can see per-kernel durations, and i've highlighted a transpose that cost ~6ms which we eliminated by changing the kv layout. small changes like that compound across layers and tokens.
00:22:35 - Priya: can Redwood help prototype kv layout changes or do we need to refactor model code?
00:22:40 - Marco: Redwood can provide adapters and a compatibility shim for model inputs that convert once at load time; full refactor is not always necessary. we'll prototype in the pilot.

00:23:10 - Sara: on the topic of CUDA Graph pitfalls \u2014 common errors include capture mismatches due to semaphore/stream usage and using non-capturable operations (like memory allocations). we recommend preallocating memory pools and avoiding cudaMalloc in the hot path.

00:24:00 - Marco: moving on to deployment recommendations: for Quasar's scale (expected 200-500 qps with bursts), a Dedicated pool with autoscaling and warm standby nodes gives the best predictable p99. if you're constrained on capex, a Private on-prem cluster with 2-3 node redundancy will also work.
00:24:30 - Lidia: any ballpark pricing differences? we'll want to compare Dedicated reserved vs Private capex.
00:24:36 - Avery: i'll send an updated throughput-based pricing sheet. rough rule: Dedicated unit cost is lower for sustained usage, Private has upfront infra cost but better long-run TCO for heavy traffic.

00:25:10 - Marco: experimental note: we tried mixed-kernel execution where some layers run in TensorRT and others in PyTorch/vLLM on the same GPU using stream parallelism \u2014 it's possible but complex; synchronization overhead often neutralizes gains. not recommended unless you have very specific layer characteristics.

00:26:00 - Daniel: is model sharding relevant here? we currently run single-GPU per model for our 13B but might move to offload for larger ones.
00:26:06 - Marco: for 13B single GPU is fine. for >70B you need tensor/model parallelism; kernel fusion and cuda graphs become more complex across sharded models. planning and testing required.

00:26:35 - Marco: demo time \u2014 i'm playing a short recording comparing t-llm int8 vs vllm fp16 (graphs) \u2014 you can see per-token jitter in vllm around token 250 when the cache window grows; t-llm is more consistent.
00:27:05 - Priya: that jitter aligns with our p99 spikes at certain prompt sizes.

00:27:40 - Marco: we also captured memory fragmentation stats; persistent allocators help reduce fragmentation so you don't have costly defrag pauses during long-run.

00:28:10 - Daniel: question: does Redwood runtime support custom allocators out of the box?
00:28:14 - Sara: yes we support custom allocator hooks, you can plug in your pool and we can manage lifetime and stats.

00:28:45 - Marco: next: fallback strategies for capacity constraints \u2014 Redwood can route to smaller model variants (eg 7B) for best-effort responses, or route to hosted replicas. this reduces tail latency when Dedicated is saturated.
00:29:05 - Lidia: acceptable for some user journeys, not for others; we'll need flexible routing rules by route.

00:29:30 - Avery: one more thing on observability \u2014 we'll attach a sample tracing dashboard that maps request id -> node -> kernel timeline so you can triage.

00:30:00 - Marco: ok we're about midway, maybe pause for clarifying questions.

00:30:10 - Daniel: can you share the exact hardware used in those numbers? A100? H100?
00:30:14 - Marco: most traces were on A100-80GB and H100 80GB; H100 shows slightly better matmul perf and reduced p99 for large GEMMs, but kernel compatibility and tensor cores optimizations vary. we'll include hardware column in the spreadsheet.

00:30:45 - Priya: do you have automation to pick kernel selection based on live perf telemetry?
00:30:50 - Marco: we have a kernel selector that can be tuned per-model and a feedback loop that suggests kernel sets based on historical traces; full auto-tuning is an ongoing feature in Redwood Optimize.

00:31:20 - Marco: showing a mode where we simulate sudden spike: we enable burst capacity to spin extra instances; observed tail reduced by ~20%. important to have autoscale headroom.

00:31:50 - Owen: latency SLO enforcement \u2014 do you p99/timeout drop with graceful degradation?
00:31:55 - Sara: yes, Redwood supports SLO-based routing: if p99 exceeds threshold we can shift to smaller model variants or restrict batch pooling to favor latency. config is per-route.

00:32:20 - Marco: back to CUDA graphs \u2014 we also instrumented the graph node list and compared runtimes; one issue we saw is memory residency for graph-captured buffers; on some drivers the capture pins memory causing higher resident memory which matters for multi-tenant setups.
00:32:45 - Priya: interesting, that could affect our cluster density.

00:33:10 - Marco: good segue \u2014 we tested density: with int4 on t-llm we could fit 2.2x more replicas per GPU vs fp16. vLLM with graphs and fp16 gave 1.6x improvement vs baseline. so quantization+fusion yields the best density.

00:33:45 - Daniel: about model updates: do you support rolling rollback with consistent cache migration?
00:33:50 - Marco: we support canary rollout with cache warmers and traffic shadowing; full consistent cache migration is hard but we do request routing to pinned warmed replicas during rollout.

00:34:20 - Priya: any caution about correctness/regression when using fused kernels? we've seen subtle numeric diffs.
00:34:26 - Marco: yes fused kernels sometimes change numerical order or precision slightly; that's why we do a calibration and quality gating step in the CI before enabling fused kernels for traffic.

00:34:55 - Sara: we'll capture the diffs and tie to evaluation thresholds; Redwood Optimize can flag regressions automatically.

00:35:20 - Marco: demo wrap-up \u2014 i'll upload the traces and the spreadsheet. next let's do an example pilot plan: week 1: baseline runs on hosted + remote traces, week 2: in-VPC pilot with 2 nodes, week 3: longer soak test with traffic mirrors.

00:36:00 - Lidia: timeline looks good; we'll confirm availability.

00:36:20 - Daniel: technical nit \u2014 for vLLM, the python layer introduces GIL/serialization overhead sometimes; did you measure that?
00:36:26 - Marco: yes it's visible when you have many tiny concurrent requests; offloading hot ops to C++ or using uvloop-like async patterns reduces it. t-llm being more native C++ has less user-space overhead.

00:36:55 - Priya: any recommendations for batching config defaults for our traffic?
00:36:59 - Marco: start with target latency 150ms, max batch size 8, batching timeout 6ms for short requests, enable batch pooling across 3 replicas. we'll tune during pilot.

00:37:30 - Marco: shown a chart: performance sensitivity to head_dim and kv layout; some models with large head dim favor different kernel shapes. we'll include per-model heuristics for Quasar's 13B.

00:37:55 - Owen: question about GPU driver versions and compatibility \u2014 anything special?
00:38:00 - Marco: we recommend recent driver + CUDA 12.x for best tensor core support. TensorRT versions also matter for int8/int4 kernels; we'll provide tested version matrix.

00:38:35 - Priya: are there any licensing ramifications using TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM?
00:38:40 - Avery: TensorRT and Nvidia binaries have their own licenses, whereas vLLM is open-source; we'll share licensing notes and our legal team can coordinate if needed.

00:39:05 - Marco: ok i'll walk through a small failure case: graph capture fails when we use a custom CUDA kernel that uses dynamic shared memory; the workaround is to pre-register and use static shared allocations or wrap the kernel outside the captured loop.

00:39:40 - Daniel: noted.

00:40:00 - Marco: final technical point \u2014 mixed precision accumulation settings can change kernel choices; enabling TF32 on H100 can give different matmul perf but can also slightly change numerical results. tradeoffs again.

00:40:30 - Priya: sounds like there are many knobs. what would you recommend as a minimal pilot to give us tangible wins?
00:40:36 - Marco: recommended pilot: 1) run baseline traces on hosted Redwood for your model; 2) run a 2-node in-VPC pilot with fp16 + cuda graphs for common shapes; 3) try int8 on a copy of model with calibration and run eval set. that should surface quick wins in p50/p99 and density.

00:41:10 - Avery: and Redwood will provide scripts to collect NVTX, per-kernel timelines, and a runbook.

00:41:35 - Lidia: ok let's capture next steps \u2014 Priya will share eval set and sample traffic, Marco will upload the traces and a recommended config.

00:42:00 - Marco: i'll also include a short checklist for VPC networking (ENIs, subnets, NACLs, KMS endpoints) so you can provision nodes ahead of the pilot.

00:42:25 - Priya: perfect. last quick question: any gotchas with container runtimes (docker vs crun) for these workloads? we've seen stability differences.
00:42:33 - Marco: use a minimal container with nvidia-container-toolkit, avoid overlayfs on heavy IO paths, and prefer crun for lower startup overhead. also pre-pull images and use pinned kernels/drivers.

00:43:10 - Daniel: on traces you shared earlier, can we get raw .nvtl/nvtx files?
00:43:14 - Marco: yes i'll upload to the shared S3 and send link.

00:43:35 - Avery: we'll also send the security checklist and the Dedicated vs Private TCO sheet.

00:44:00 - Priya: thanks everyone. any other technical points?

00:44:08 - Owen: one thought \u2014 we have upcoming audit in Q1, we'd like to validate telemetry retention and KMS integration as part of pilot.
00:44:15 - Avery: noted, we'll include audit retention options in the doc we send.

00:44:40 - Marco: quick mention of multi-model routing: if you have smaller models for certain routes we can set up per-route routing rules and make sure caches are warmed on each variant.

00:45:05 - Daniel: good \u2014 we'll think about which routes are latency-critical.

00:45:30 - Priya: any final notes about quantization fallback? if int4 causes quality drop do you have a fast rollback?
00:45:36 - Marco: yes we usually run small % of traffic on quantized variant and monitor scores; if drop detected we rollback at routing layer. the rollback can be immediate because models are versioned and we can pin traffic to previous variant.

00:46:10 - Lidia: thanks Marco.

00:46:20 - Marco: ok i'm going to summarize: action items (we listed), pilot plan (3 weeks), deliverables (traces, spreadsheet, security checklist). i'll send calendar invite for the pilot kick-off.

00:46:45 - Avery: thanks all, really appreciate the detailed conversation. any final quick questions?
00:46:52 - Priya: not from me. we'll aim to provide the traffic samples by Friday.

00:47:05 - Marco: thanks everyone, we'll follow up.
